Let’s get into Chapter 7: Negotiating with Difficult People—how to handle hard bargainers and those infamous dirty tricks.
You know, not every negotiation is going to feel like a friendly team effort. Sometimes, you’ll run into folks who play rough—people who use aggressive tactics, bend the truth, or even try to manipulate you just to come out on top.
These “hard bargainers” might refuse to budge, throw out wild demands, or try to pressure you with threats and ultimatums. So, what do you do when things get tough?
The most important thing is to stay calm and clear-headed. Don’t let yourself get sucked into a battle of egos or start playing their game. Instead, keep your focus on the process and the real problem—not on personalities.
Let’s look at some common tactics you might face:
First, there’s extreme demands—people start way outside the realm of reasonable, hoping to anchor the negotiation in their favor. Then, there’s stonewalling—refusing to give an inch or even talk about solutions. Some folks go for personal attacks, trying to shake your confidence. Others might use deception, twisting facts or hiding their true intentions. And of course, there are pressure tactics—think threats, ticking clocks, or “take-it-or-leave-it” offers.
So, how do you handle these? Here’s what works:
First, recognize the tactic for what it is. Sometimes just naming it to yourself—or even gently pointing it out—takes away its power.
Next, don’t let your emotions take over. Stay cool, even when things get heated. That way, you won’t escalate the conflict or lose your footing.
Try to reframe the conversation. Bring things back to interests, options, and real, objective standards—rather than getting stuck on positions or personalities.
If the process itself feels unfair, speak up and suggest some ground rules, or propose a different approach.
And always remember your BATNA—that’s your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If things get too one-sided or even abusive, be ready to walk away. Sometimes, that’s your strongest move.
For example, let’s say someone throws down a “take-it-or-leave-it” offer. Instead of getting flustered, you might calmly ask them to explain their reasoning, or invite them to work with you on finding a fair standard.
If you’re on the receiving end of a personal attack, you can acknowledge their emotion, but gently steer the talk back to the real issues at hand.
Here’s a strategy I love—“go to the balcony.” It’s just a way of saying, step back mentally and look at the situation from above. This pause helps you keep perspective and choose your next move thoughtfully, instead of reacting on impulse.
And remember, being a principled negotiator doesn’t mean you’re naïve or passive. It means you assertively protect your interests and the negotiation process, but you don’t get pulled into games or power struggles.
By sticking to fair standards and knowing your BATNA, you shield yourself—and sometimes, you even encourage the other side to behave more constructively.
